books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, B. Cotton, Slavery, and the Southern Exception

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, 1835

stimulus.text:
Alexis de Tocqueville, a French visitor, traveled in the United States in 1831-1832 and published Democracy in America in 1835. Crossing the Ohio River, he compared the slave state of Kentucky with the free state of Ohio:

“These two States only differ in a single respect; Kentucky has admitted slavery, but the State of Ohio has prohibited the existence of slaves within its borders. . . . Upon the left bank of the stream the population is rare; from time to time one descries a troop of slaves loitering in the half-desert fields; the primaeval forest recurs at every turn; society seems to be asleep, man to be idle, and nature alone offers a scene of activity and of life. From the right bank, on the contrary, a confused hum is heard which proclaims the presence of industry; the fields are covered with abundant harvests.”

“Upon the left bank of the Ohio labor is confounded with the idea of slavery, upon the right bank it is identified with that of prosperity and improvement; on the one side it is degraded, on the other it is honored; on the former territory no white laborers can be found, for they would be afraid of assimilating themselves to the negroes.”

Tocqueville adds that the 1830 census counted 688,844 people in Kentucky and 937,679 in Ohio.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18, as printed on americanliterature.com (full text) and historycarper.com. Census figures as given by Tocqueville in the same chapter.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, 1835, public domain
stem: A historian using Tocqueville's comparison should be most careful about which limit?

options.text: Tocqueville wrote in French, so his words cannot be translated
options.misconception: Democracy in America was translated into English in his own lifetime and is widely read in translation.

options.text: Tocqueville never visited Kentucky or Ohio, so he could only guess at the difference
options.misconception: Tocqueville traveled the Ohio valley in 1831 and describes crossing the river himself.

options.text: The two states had the same population in 1830
options.misconception: Tocqueville gives the 1830 census: 688,844 in Kentucky and 937,679 in Ohio.

options.text: The two states differed in more than slavery, such as age and settlement

rationales.A: Democracy in America was translated into English in his own lifetime and is widely read in translation.
rationales.B: Tocqueville traveled the Ohio valley in 1831 and describes crossing the river himself.
rationales.C: Tocqueville gives the 1830 census: 688,844 in Kentucky and 937,679 in Ohio.
rationales.D: Kentucky was settled earlier than Ohio, and the states differed in roads, towns, and trade as well as in slavery, so slavery alone may not explain every difference.
rationales.general:
1. Test each option against the passage. Tocqueville did visit, did give different census figures, and was translated.
2. Ask what else differs. Kentucky was founded in 1775, Ohio twelve years later, so their settlement histories differ.
3. Name the limit. A two-state comparison can suggest a cause, but it cannot prove slavery caused every difference.
Background: Tocqueville himself warns that the states differ in age, which is why he names the dates.
Remember: a comparison proves most when the two sides differ in only one way.
